title: Money & Economics Shorts
chapters: Inequality: how the gap between rich and poor is measured
The market for lemons: when sellers know more than buyers

units.t: Money & Economics Shorts.
In this episode: Inequality: how the gap between rich and poor is measured and The market for lemons: when sellers know more than buyers.
Part one. Inequality: how the gap between rich and poor is measured.
Is the gap between rich and poor growing?
The answer depends on what you measure, and economists have been arguing about it for more than a century.
Income versus wealth.
Talk about inequality often blurs two different things.
Income is money that comes in over a period, from wages, business profits, interest, rent or government payments.
Wealth is the stock of what you own minus what you owe: a house, superannuation, shares, savings and a car, less any mortgage or debts.
A young doctor might have a high income but little wealth, while a retired farmer could have modest income and substantial wealth in land.
Across almost every country, wealth is far more unequally distributed than income.
Wealth builds up over a lifetime, earns its own returns and can be passed on, so differences tend to compound over time.
The Gini coefficient.
In 1905 the American economist Max Lorenz proposed a neat way to picture inequality.
Line everyone up from poorest to richest and plot what share of total income the bottom 10 per cent, 20 per cent and so on receive.
If everyone earned the same, the line would be perfectly straight.
The more it sags, the more unequal the society.
In 1912 the Italian statistician Corrado Gini turned this into a single number.
A Gini coefficient of 0 means perfect equality, and 1 means one person has everything.
Most developed countries have income Gini figures between roughly 0.
25 and 0.
40, and wealth figures that are considerably higher.
When averages mislead.
Around 1900, Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto studied tax and property records from several countries and centuries.
He found the top of the distribution followed a similar pattern again and again, with a small share of people holding a large share of the total.
The popular eighty-twenty rule was named after him, though it is far looser than his mathematics.
This power law still describes the top of wealth distributions well.
It means averages can mislead.
If a billionaire walks into a pub, the average wealth soars, yet nobody else is richer.
Economists often prefer the median, the person exactly in the middle, to the mean.
They also compare the 90th and 10th percentiles, or track the top 1 per cent's income share.
Kuznets, Piketty and debate.
In 1955 economist Simon Kuznets suggested that inequality rises as countries industrialise and then falls as they mature, an upside-down U called the Kuznets curve.
The mid-twentieth century seemed to prove him right, as gaps narrowed in many rich countries.
Then, from around 1980, top income shares rose again in the United States, Britain and elsewhere.
In 2013 French economist Thomas Piketty published Capital in the Twenty-First Century, arguing that when the return on capital exceeds the growth rate of the economy, wealth tends to concentrate.
His book became a surprise bestseller and drew strong criticism, with economists still debating his data, his theory and his proposed wealth taxes.
Can you climb the ladder.
A snapshot of inequality does not say whether the same people stay at the top or bottom.
Economic mobility asks how strongly your adult income is linked to your parents' income.
Research led by economist Miles Corak found that countries with higher inequality tend to have lower mobility between generations, a link dubbed the Great Gatsby curve by Alan Krueger in 2012.
It is a correlation, and researchers debate what drives it, from education and housing to social networks.
Measured mobility in Australia has generally been found to be higher than in the United States, though comparing countries is tricky.
Many people care less about the gap itself than about whether the ladder is climbable.
The key idea: Income is what flows in each year; wealth is what you own, and it is usually far more unequal.
Part two. The market for lemons: when sellers know more than buyers.
A short paper about dodgy used cars was rejected by several journals.
It went on to win a Nobel Prize and explain why some markets break down.
Peaches and lemons.
In the United States a defective car is called a lemon, and a good one a peach.
In 1970 economist George Akerlof used used cars to explore a powerful idea.
The seller knows the car's history.
The buyer usually does not.
Economists call this asymmetric information.
If buyers cannot tell peaches from lemons, they offer only an average price.
To the owner of a genuine peach, that is too low, so many decide not to sell.
That leaves more lemons, buyers lower their offers further, and more good cars leave.
In the extreme, the market collapses until only lemons remain, or no trade happens at all, even though buyers would gladly pay a fair price for a good car.
Rejected, then rewarded.
The paper had a rocky start.
Akerlof later recounted that several leading journals rejected it, with reviewers suggesting it was too trivial or, alternatively, that if it were correct, economics would be different.
It was eventually published in the Quarterly Journal of Economics in 1970.
Over time it became one of the most cited papers in the field, because the idea applied far beyond cars.
In 2001 Akerlof shared the Nobel Prize in economics with Michael Spence and Joseph Stiglitz, who had developed related ideas about how markets cope with hidden information.
Together their work helped launch the economics of information, which now underpins thinking about insurance, lending and online trade.
Adverse selection.
Insurance shows the lemons problem in reverse.
The buyer of health insurance often knows more about their own health than the insurer does.
If premiums are set at an average level, people who expect to need lots of care find the deal attractive, while healthy people may decide it is not worth it.
As the healthy leave, the insured pool gets sicker and more expensive, premiums rise and still more healthy people drop out.
This spiral is called adverse selection.

Australia's Lifetime Health Cover, introduced in 2000, tackles it by adding a loading to private hospital cover premiums for people who first take out cover later in life, from their early thirties on, encouraging people to join while young and healthy.
Signals and screens.
Markets are not helpless.
Michael Spence showed how the informed side can send a signal, an action that is costly for low-quality sellers to fake.
A dealer who offers a long warranty on a used car signals confidence, since honouring it on a lemon would be expensive.
Spence's best-known example was education: a degree may signal persistence and ability to employers, whatever its direct usefulness.
Joseph Stiglitz showed how the less informed side can screen, for instance by offering a menu of insurance policies with different excesses, so customers reveal their own risk by what they choose.
Brand reputations, independent inspections and vehicle history reports all do the same job, making hidden quality visible.
Lemons everywhere.
Once you see the lemons problem, it appears everywhere.
Online marketplaces rely on ratings and reviews so strangers can trust each other, and fake reviews are damaging precisely because they poison those signals.
Lenders check credit histories because borrowers know more about their own finances.
Employers ask for references.
Consumer protection laws, including statutory guarantees that goods must be of acceptable quality, give buyers some assurance and reduce the advantage of sellers who hide defects.
Akerlof's insight was that missing information is not a minor detail.
It can stop a market working at all.
Much of the machinery of modern commerce, from warranties to watchdogs, exists to close that gap.
The key idea: When sellers know far more than buyers, good products can be driven out of a market.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why is wealth usually more unequal than income?
Answer. It compounds and can be inherited.
Question two. In Akerlof's model, why might good cars disappear from the market?
Answer. Average prices are too low for their owners.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
